title: Hausdorff separation
terms: Hausdorff space; separation of points; uniqueness of limits; T1 separation; cofinite topol- ogy; cocountable topology.

exposition.text:
A space is Hausdorff if distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods. Every metric space is
Hausdorff. Hausdorff spaces have closed singletons and unique limits of convergent sequences,
though those latter properties alone should not be substituted for the definition in arbitrary
spaces.
Every compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed. A finite Hausdorff space is discrete: for
each point, intersect finitely many open neighborhoods that exclude each other point. The
Hausdorff hypothesis is essential in many compactness and homeomorphism statements.
A T space is one in which every singleton is closed. The cofinite topology consists of the empty
1
set and sets with finite complement; the cocountable topology replaces finite by countable.
On an infinite cofinite space, disjoint nonempty open sets do not exist. On an uncountable
cocountable space the same obstruction holds, although every convergent sequence is eventually
constant.

question.text:
A Hausdorff topology is placed on a set of five points. How many open sets does it have?
(A) 5 (B) 6 (C) 10 (D) 16 (E) 32

solution.text:
For a fixed point x, separate x from each of the other four points and intersect the four
neighborhoods of x. This makes {x} open. Every singleton is open, hence every subset is
5
open; there are 2 = 32.

question.text:
Let X be Hausdorff, let K ⊆ X be compact, and suppose (x ) in K converges in X to x.
n
Which must hold?
(A) x is isolated in K. (B) K is finite. (C) x ∈ K. (D) K is open. (E) X is compact.

solution.text:
The compact subset K is closed because X is Hausdorff, so its complement cannot contain
the limit of a sequence lying in K. None of finiteness, isolation, openness, or compactness
of the whole space follows.

question.text:
A convergent sequence in a Hausdorff space has
(A) An open range
(B) At most one limit
(C) An eventually constant tail
(D) Only finitely many distinct terms
(E) Exactly one isolated point in its range

solution.text:
Two distinct proposed limits have disjoint neighborhoods. Convergence would force every
sufficiently late term into both neighborhoods, a contradiction. The sequence need not be
eventually constant.

question.text:
An uncountable set X has the topology consisting of ∅ and sets with countable complement.
Which statement is correct?
(A) X is Hausdorff.
(B) Every sequence converges to every point.
(C) X is not Hausdorff, but every convergent sequence has a unique limit.
(D) Every singleton is open.
(E) Some sequence has two distinct limits.

solution.text:
Any two nonempty open sets intersect, because the union of their countable complements
cannot exhaust uncountable X. Thus the space is not Hausdorff. If x → x, remove the
n
countable set of all terms different from x; its complement is an open neighborhood of
x. Convergence forces the sequence eventually to equal x, so a second limit is impossible.
Uniqueness of sequence limits alone does not characterize Hausdorff spaces.
